Abandoned
This much is obvious from the code.  Please explain -why- we should prefer the approach with additional indirection and dependencies for a string constant.

I don't see the value in repeating a rather extensive reasoning and justification in 20+ patches and bloating the git log of various repositories.

Since the complete reasoning has already been provided in multiple places. If there is a disagreement with said reasoning i am happy to discuss.

https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#es45-avoid-magic-constants-use-symbolic-constants

> with additional indirection

I don't see indirection as the problem here.
There was already indirection before as `assocDefsInterface` was defined and the string literal was not inlined.

The conventional using-declaration provides consistency since it is the same for a given interface, even across different repositories.

Even if we have one more level of indirection due to the using-declaration, IMO the result is easier to understand than before.

> and dependencies

Even if you do not declare PDI as a compile-time dependency directly, the dependency still exists.

Similarly, if we write a linux userspace application, we have a compile-time dependency on the linux syscall interface.

If the mapper interfaces experience breaking changes in PDI, then the code here should fail to compile.

> I don't see the value

The request for why was somewhat tongue-in-cheek.
I don't have a problem with these constants.

> I don't have a problem with these constants.

Do you think they make the code better?  This isn't enabling some feature for the submitter...its just a refactor so there should be some benefit.  What is it?
Something on my todo list has actually been to remove the pdi dependency from the mapper.

> Something on my todo list has actually been to remove the pdi dependency from the mapper.

Elaborating...I sort of understand the desire in other OpenBMC projects.  But the mapper follows the conventions of typical dbus application programming where the service schema is defined and discovered by the well known service name.  It will never make dbus calls to other openbmc services and thus the whole 'check the api at build time' is not applicable.

> Something on my todo list has actually been to remove the pdi dependency from the mapper.

To what end? Does it meaningfully improve the build time?

If the PDI headers introduce too much overhead then that's something we can try to improve. Let me know if there is an issue there.

Or are you more concerned with reducing the amount of dependencies?

> It will never make dbus calls to other openbmc services and thus the whole 'check the api at build time' is not applicable.

Mapper depends on the `xyz.openbmc_project.Association.Definitions` interface, which is defined in PDI. So we have a dependency on that definition.

We can manually copy-paste the information about the interface into the application or simply use the generated header. Using the generated header is more convenient IMO.

Mapper also has a dependency on the `xyz.openbmc_project.Association` interface which it must create. Which is also defined in the PDI. So there is also a dependency there.

No, the one time cost of building PDI when hacking on the mapper is not really a big deal (although it isn't nothing).

I don't like how PDI effectively destroys incremental builds.  The more applications we add it to the worse it gets.

> I don't like how PDI effectively destroys incremental builds.  The more applications we add it to the worse it gets.

For full image builds, yes, a small bump in PDI can trigger lots of recipes to be rebuilt. Even if the interface definitions which were updated are unrelated to the recipe.

Essentially a tooling limitation, maybe some yocto expert can tell how to fix it?

But IMO that's just the spirit of C++. Even for small improvements to the code, people are willing to take on a large build time hit and resource consumption.


Consider a few minutes of extra build time against the possibility that 2 weeks into an image being deployed, in some rarely used code path there is a hardcoded usage of some interface, with property name typo or data type mixup, which just crashes the whole reactor.
